# Meaning and Truth: Reference, Checking and Hallucination {#sec-ch-meaning-and-truth}

A sense is not a truth value. Frege's three levels end in the reference, the object that a sign picks out, and the reference of a sentence is its truth value; the thought alone, he says, yields no knowledge, but only the thought together with its reference [@frege1892sense]. A space trained on text has the sense at best, and the question of this chapter is how far it can go towards the reference and the truth: how a name is tied to its bearer (Kripke and Putnam [@kripke1980naming; @putnam1975meaning]), whether "true" adds anything to what is asserted (Ramsey [@ramsey1927facts]), what a model that is built to produce what is plausible does when it is not true (hallucination), and what it takes to check a text: against sources, against itself, by proof. The chapter also keeps a question that the chapter on difference leaves open: can a representation reach "false" by derivation and keep it apart from "unknown"?

The scope is reference and truth. The dependence of a sentence on its situation is the chapter on context (@sec-ch-meaning-in-context); the production of plausible text is the chapter on generation (@sec-ch-meaning-as-generation), from which this chapter takes the contrast between plausible and true; a negation as a vector operation is the chapter on difference (@sec-ch-meaning-as-difference); and whether a space can be grounded by another sense is the chapter on senses (@sec-ch-meaning-across-senses).

*Goals and expectations (proposed, to be confirmed by the author before any experiment).*

*Goal 1, a name and its bearer (Kripke, Putnam).* The expectation is that nearness follows the company of a name and not its bearer: names with a widespread false description sit near the description, a name with two bearers has one vector that averages them, and two names for one object are near only if their company is. The first run is the one of the chapter on nearness (@sec-near-not-alike); this chapter carries its result on, and adds a test with a contextual model, which sees the sentence that the name is in (@sec-truth-bearer). *This goal receives Q16 of @sec-likeness-which.*

*Goal 2, a direction of truth.* There are linear structures of truth with causal interventions [@marks2024geometry] and unsupervised directions [@burns2023discovering], and probes that fail to generalize [@levinstein2023still] and a warning that the method may find the most prominent feature and not truth [@farquhar2023challenges]. The expectation is that a direction fitted on one set of true and false statements separates them there and generalizes worse to another set, and that a direction that separates true from commonly asserted differs from one that separates true from false. The run needs activations of an open language model and labelled statements (@sec-truth-direction). *This goal receives Q16 of @sec-likeness-which.*

*Goal 3, plausible and true (the contrast with generation).* A model that defines a density over text produces what is typical. The expectation is that the likelihood of a statement under a language model tracks its truth less well than it tracks how common it is. The run compares the log-likelihood of true and false statements, matched for frequency (@sec-plausible-true).

*Goal 4, checking against a source.* Retrieval-augmented generation grounds a text in sources that can be checked. The expectation is that it reduces unsupported claims in the answers to questions about single facts, and not in the answers that need negation, conjunction or several hops [@karpukhin2020dense]. The run is a toy retrieval over a small set of documents (@sec-negation-multi-hop-reasoning).

*Goal 5, reaching "false" (an idea).* Falsehood is not the absence of truth: it is a conclusion, reached from ground truth and common sense, and it must be told from ignorance. A verdict has at least three values (entailed, refuted, undetermined), and a four-valued logic reads them as two independent axes, evidence for and evidence against, whose corners are true, false, both and neither. The expectation is that a representation which returns the three verdicts exists only if containment or orthogonality of concepts is used, and that a single score collapses refuted and undetermined. The run, if kept, is a toy with premises and rules (@sec-reaching-false, @sec-truth-logics).

## What the Philosophies Say About Truth {#sec-truth-philosophy}
*Plan (about 4 pages). Frege: sense, reference and the truth value of a sentence, and the sentence without reference [@frege1892sense]; Russell's descriptions [@russell1905denoting] and Kripke's attack on the description theory of names [@kripke1980naming]; Putnam's Twin Earth, "meanings ain't in the head" [@putnam1975meaning]; Ramsey's redundancy view and his meaning by consequences [@ramsey1927facts]; Tarski's semantic conception [@tarski1944semantic]; the argument from form [@bender2020climbing; @searle1980minds]; and grounding [@harnad1990symbol]. For each: what truth or reference would be, what a vector carries of it, and where it stops. The correspondence reading of a truth direction (it tracks facts) and the coherence or deflationary readings (it tracks what is asserted, or only endorses a sentence) are kept apart.*

## Does a Sense Know Its Bearer? {#sec-truth-bearer}
*Plan (about 2 pages). Goal 1. The three kinds of name of the chapter on nearness (a false description, two bearers, two names for one object), now with a contextual model that sees the sentence; the ground truth of "the bearer" comes from outside the corpus and is declared.*

## Is There a Direction of Truth? {#sec-truth-direction}
*Plan (about 3 pages). Goal 2. A probe of the activations of a small open model for true and false statements, its generalization to a second set, the control task, and the separation of true from commonly asserted. The claim that truth directions diverge from what is commonly believed has no source in the collection and is not to be stated before one is read.*

## Plausible Is Not True {#sec-plausible-true}
*Plan (1 page). Findings: what a distribution over the data adds to a map (sampling, a score, a decoder with a geometry of its own), and what the reconciliation with the predictive and reconstructive models of @sec-ch-meaning-as-likeness found: a common currency in information, and the places where the two families stay different. Achieved for the representation of meaning: a point can now be drawn and a path decoded (@sec-prop-paths), and the pullback metric says when the midpoint of two codes means anything (@sec-prop-region). Computation: a decoder prices every detail, prediction without a decoder prices only what separates the negatives; whether generation absorbs the maps of @sec-ch-meaning-as-likeness, prediction without a decoder absorbs generation, or both survive because they answer different questions (what you can get back and sample, against what you can compare) is read from evidence kept in separate classes: a position paper [@lecun2022path], scaled generative results, and the chapter's own small experiment. Evidence at scale: no controlled comparison independent of the proponents is known to the author, and the chapter says so if the search finds none. The small experiment (embedding-technologies-stubs/README.md, section embedding_spaces) is a smoke test, with its beta fixed by a rule before retrieval is computed. It can falsify a claim and cannot rank the families at scale. Reading, dated 2026: undecided unless the evidence moves. Still out of reach: a model that samples produces what is plausible without checking it, which is where hallucination comes from. The hidden vectors of such a model are the contextual vectors of @sec-ch-meaning-in-context, read from inside, and @sec-ch-meaning-and-truth takes up the remedy of looking up what is known.*

## Reaching "False" {#sec-reaching-false}
*Falsehood is not the absence of truth: it is a conclusion, reached from ground truth and common sense, and it must be told from ignorance. Three verdicts: entailed, refuted (the negation is entailed), undetermined. Test (internal consistency in the critical literacy test): given premises and rules, does a representation return all three, or does it collapse "refuted" and "undetermined" into one low score? Geometric hypothesis to test: if a concept is a region or subspace, entailment is containment, exclusion is disjointness (orthogonality for subspaces), and partial overlap is undetermined; chains such as $A \subseteq B$ and $B \perp C$ then give $A \perp C$ without any rule. What geometry may not reach: uniqueness constraints ("a country has one capital") and rules with variables, which need binding (@sec-ch-meaning-and-structure) or an external reasoner. Common sense is defeasible, so a conclusion of falsehood drawn from it is too. Whether the closed-world default (what is not derivable is false) or the open-world one (it is unknown) is assumed changes the verdict, and the test states which.*

Two origins now read: Frege's truth value as the reference of a sentence [@frege1892sense] and Ramsey's redundancy view, that "it is true that Caesar was murdered" means no more than that Caesar was murdered ([@ramsey1927facts, p. 157]), so that a verdict "refuted" is the assertion of the negation and not a further predicate; containment boxes as a candidate geometry for entailment [@vilnis2018probabilistic].

Sources (first pass, none yet in `references.bib`; read before citing). Reiter on the closed-world assumption and default logic; Belnap's four-valued logic; order embeddings (Vendrov et al. 2016) and box embeddings for containment; logic tensor networks for truth degrees; three-way reasoning benchmarks with an "unknown" answer (ProofWriter, FOLIO), and NLI with its neutral class. All from memory, to be checked.

## More Than Two Verdicts {#sec-truth-logics}
*Plan (about 2 pages; an idea, kept only if a vector construction separates the verdicts and does not just label them). Classical logic puts every claim on one line, true or false. Belnap's four-valued logic reads a claim by two independent axes, evidence for and evidence against, so that its values are true, false, both and neither (to be read at the source; not in `references/`); paraconsistent and dialetheist logics allow a claim to be both [@priest2002beyond], the Buddhist tetralemma has the same four corners [@nagarjuna1995fundamental], and non-monotonic logics (default reasoning, circumscription) are about revising a verdict, which is a path in the space of the chapter on paths. Two coordinates are what a vector represents naturally. The test, if the idea is kept: a model with two probes, one for evidence for and one for evidence against, on premises that are contradictory, silent and consistent; do the four corners separate, or does the model collapse "both" and "neither" into one low score? Sources to be read before any prose: Belnap, Priest, Reiter on default logic.*

## Technologies That Exploit Truth {#sec-truth-technologies}
*Plan (about 1 page). Retrieval-augmented generation and the vector databases and approximate-search indexes behind it, checking against knowledge graphs, internal-consistency checks and self-verification, proof assistants and neural theorem proving, and truth probes. Vector databases are one technology among several for one problem; the others are listed with their own costs. For each: the cost per query, and whether the evidence at scale shows fewer unsupported claims at matched tuning.*

## Remembering Is Not Knowing {#sec-remembering-knowing}
*Plan (1 page). Findings: why distance concentration forces approximate search, what a fixed-dimension dot product can and cannot rank, and how retrieval-augmented generation behaved on negation, conjunction and multi-hop questions, told as a dated case study. Achieved for the representation of meaning: nearness (@sec-prop-nearness) at the scale of billions, and a memory outside the weights that grounds generation in text that can be checked. Computation: search can be paid once in training and amortized into the weights, or paid at every query, the same trade as for reasoning in @sec-ch-meaning-in-context. Parametric memory is the amortized side, retrieval and agentic search the per-query side, and which is cheaper depends on the difficulty of the question and the compute available [@snell2024scaling; @jones2021scaling]. Whether long contexts and agentic search absorb retrieval, or external memory survives on cost, is open and dated. Evidence at scale: benchmark comparisons of approximate-search indexes and of dense against lexical retrieval exist (from memory, to be checked: ANN-Benchmarks and BEIR), and the dense-retrieval paper held in references/ (Karpukhin et al.) is the authors' own comparison. Smoke tests: recall against query time of exact and approximate search on random and on clustered vectors, which shows distance concentration directly, and a count of the rankings that a query vector of dimension 2 and 3 can realize over a small set of items. Still out of reach: a retrieved passage is not a checked claim, and one vector per item cannot negate or chain. Checking a text against verified sources is the external-consistency question of the critical literacy test, and keeping the structure of a subject is taken up by the extensions that follow, beginning with curvature in @sec-ch-meaning-as-generation.*

*Sources and gaps (first pass).* Sourced in `references/`: Frege, Kripke, Putnam, Ramsey, Russell, the argument from form and grounding, truth directions and their sceptics, dense retrieval. Not yet sourced: Belnap and Reiter (the logics section rests on them); Tarski at the page; a corpus of true and false statements for the probe; the claim that truth directions diverge from common belief; benchmark comparisons of retrieval methods named in the earlier chapter (from memory, not read).

## Meaning Is Tied to the World, and a Sense Is Not a Truth Value {#sec-prop-truth}
*A vector gives the sense; whether a name picks out its bearer and whether a sentence is true are further facts, and a model that produces the plausible can produce the false.*

Earned in this chapter. Last update: 2026-11-22, a promise.

Sources (first pass). Frege on sense, reference and truth value [@frege1892sense]; Kripke and Putnam on names and natural kinds [@kripke1980naming; @putnam1975meaning]; Ramsey on the redundancy of truth [@ramsey1927facts]; the argument from form [@bender2020climbing]; truth directions and their sceptics [@marks2024geometry; @burns2023discovering; @levinstein2023still; @farquhar2023challenges]. Sceptics and balance: whether a truth direction tracks facts or only what the text asserts is open.
